newsitem.title: USA: Sharp U.S. Feb PPI slide soothes inflation jitters.
newsitem.headline: Sharp U.S. Feb PPI slide soothes inflation jitters.

text.p: A surprisingly sharp slide in February wholesale prices reinforced the widespread notion that U.S. inflation remains dormant, a situation that could allow the Federal Reserve to keep monetary policy on hold, economists said.
However, the good news for the credit markets was partially offset by continued pipeline inflation pressures in core crude and intermediate goods, analysts said.
"There is something here for both sides of the (Federal Reserve) policy debate," said economist Alan Levenson.

"On the one hand, the headline numbers were very tame. On the other hand, pipeline inflation pressures continue to brew with the trend rates year-to-year of core crude and core intermediate goods both widening. We think the Fed will react to these inflation pressures while the headline remains tame," UBS Securities' Levenson added.

The Department of Labor's Producer Price Index (PPI) fell 0.4 percent in February -- the largest drop since October of 1994 and well below Wall Street expectations for a 0.1 percent loss. The January figure was unrevised at a 0.3 percent drop.
A back-to-back monthly drop in the index has not occurred since September and October 1994, the Department said.

The core rate, which excludes the more volatile food and energy components, fell a seasonally adjusted 0.1 percent versus a flat reading in January. Core crude goods rose 1.0 percent compared to a 2.0 percent rise in January.
"It's an excellent number and it was surprising to see such a unanimous reading," said Kathleen Stephansen, senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
"Industrial prices had gone up (last month) but it now appears there will be no further rise," she added.
Manufacturing materials fell 0.1 percent in February after rising 0.1 percent the prior month.
Some economists said the report could trouble Fed governors at their March 25 monetary policy-setting meeting.

"The inflation numbers are just too tame for (the Fed) to tighten. It really puts them in a dilemma. I think they need at least one bad inflation number before they can pull the trigger," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities.
"It's literally verging on the miraculous that we continue to run with robust economic growth but no evidence of inflation and you need that evidence before they can go," he added.
John Park, an economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co, said a large 1.2 percent fall in February energy prices was the main force pushing the overall index into negative territory.
"This whole thing is pretty much energy. If you look away from energy, it doesn't look so benign," Park said.
The 30-year Treasury bond jumped over half a point in a knee-jerk reaction to the report, but soon pared its gains.

Meanwhile, the dollar dipped against the mark but held steady versus the yen while the report buoyed stocks at the open. The Dow Jones industrials gained over 40 points in early trade after a precipitous fall of over 160 points on Thursday.
